title: Prove Yazelix Eon as a thin orchestrator
description:
Goal:
Prove Eon as a thin orchestrator assembled from exact accepted Orbit, Venus, Helix, Yazi, and Ratconfig inputs while preserving one owner for each behavior.

Current state and planning-container boundary:
The user activated Eon through eon-68v. eon-omq proved the canonical component manifest, and eon-ax4 proved the accepted Nix-only Linux alpha. On 2026-08-08 the user selected eon-pxn, approved and indexed EON-C8, and activated only eon-pxn.1 as the topology/action implementation child. This epic remains a deferred planning container and must not be claimed; every other child frontier remains inactive.

Chosen repository boundary:
Orbit, Venus, and Eon remain separate repositories with clean ownership, histories, forkability, and independent experimentation. Orbit owns generic terminal sessions and state. Venus owns native graphical materialization. Eon owns product workspace topology, orchestration, composition, policy, diagnostics, updates, and distribution. Cross-repository contracts pin exact revisions; Eon does not copy child schemas or behavior. Yazelix Nova remains independent.

Contracts:
EON-C1 through EON-C4 describe the accepted alpha. EON-C5 through EON-C8 remain planned or decision-gated child scope. This epic itself creates no runtime contract.

Sequence:
1. eon-68v accepted the exact Orbit and Venus handoffs and activated Eon.
2. eon-omq proved one distribution-neutral component manifest.
3. eon-ax4 proved, dogfooded, and reconciled the smallest Nix-only Linux composition.
4. After the alpha and child graduations, the user selected eon-pxn as the single next frontier. EON-C8 is indexed as Planned, and eon-pxn.1 is its sole active implementation child.
5. Direct distribution begins only through eon-p93 and then eon-ohh; Home Manager and macOS remain separately gated by eon-omv and eon-hzq.
6. Editor replacement, isolated execution targets, and extensions remain decision-only work in eon-ofb, eon-az9, and eon-ix6 after their dogfood prerequisites.

Success:
Eon stays a small product-policy, workspace, composition, diagnostics, and distribution owner. Exact child revisions and focused checks prove useful vertical slices without creating a second terminal, renderer, editor, file manager, configuration system, protocol schema, package graph, or extension runtime.

comments.text:
Reference gate — alternate desktop identity under EON-C1

Question: How should Eon package a second launcher identity without creating a second runtime owner or duplicating the canonical desktop-entry policy?
Contract: EON-C1 only. Selecting “Eon (Alternate Icon)” must invoke the same `eon` executable and retain `StartupWMClass=yazelix-venus`; only desktop-file ID, display name, and icon name differ.
Sources and revisions: current `flake.nix` desktop owner at Eon HEAD 2b8fef19bb09d7ea0d1e891720eb36c838cbd237; Nixpkgs `pkgs/build-support/make-desktopitem/default.nix` at pinned revision 567a49d1913ce81ac6e9582e3553dd90a955875f; Nixpkgs RustDesk package at that revision as a comparable multiple-`desktopItems` implementation; user-owned source `assets/icon-concepts/icon_eon_3.png`, SHA-256 1bc63f18c821520e9a3b5e09f1c8bd5e33b5a87da85179523cb22bc1fb0d9786, 1254x1254 RGB.
Constraints preserved: `makeDesktopItem` renders and runs `desktop-file-validate`; it is explicitly `lib.makeOverridable`, so the established canonical derivation can own all shared fields and a sibling override can change only `name`, `desktopName`, and `icon`. `copyDesktopItems` accepts a list. Both launchers retain `Exec=eon`, categories, keywords, terminal policy, and WM grouping. The canonical `assets/eon.png` and `eon.desktop` remain unchanged.
Options compared: no second entry (rejects the explicit request); duplicate a full `makeDesktopItem` attrset (works but creates duplicate launcher policy); add a desktop action to the canonical entry (not a separate desktop entry and cannot supply an independently selectable application icon); override the existing derivation (selected).
Decision: prepare one transparent `assets/eon-alternate.png`; create `eon-alternate.desktop` by overriding the canonical desktop item only at the three identity fields; install both icons through the existing Nix package.
Rejected alternatives and failure conditions: replacing the canonical icon violates the requested sibling identity; a second executable/configuration/product duplicates runtime ownership; SVG tracing or new icon tooling adds unsupported geometry and dependencies.
Cheapest proof: image metadata/alpha checks, exact generated desktop-file field comparison plus `desktop-file-validate`, pinned flake evaluation/build, installed-icon comparison, and `git diff --check`.
Exit condition: the second entry and prepared icon validate and package while canonical entry/icon metadata and the Eon component graph remain unchanged.

title: Audit the canonical Eon component graph
description:
## Contract routing

This is a read-only repository audit. It changes no EON product contract, implements no feature or fix, and authorizes no dependency, compatibility surface, or public behavior. Audit one exact accepted revision and preserve all pre-existing worktree state.

## Why

Feature-local fresh-eyes and simplification passes can converge while stable identities, compatibility edges, validation, and consumers can drift into duplicate graphs. This subsystem owns a distinct invariant and failure domain, so it needs one bounded whole-subsystem review that includes direct callers and consumers.

## Evidence

- `components/eon-alpha-v1.json:1`: one distribution-neutral graph records the alpha composition
- `crates/eon-manifest/src/lib.rs:129`: the validator is the graph acceptance owner
- `crates/eon-manifest/src/lib.rs:171`: semantic compatibility validation is centralized
- `flake.nix:52`: Nix consumes the canonical JSON graph

## Prerequisites and reference gate

- There is no planning dependency beyond a stable in-scope subject. Do not start while another issue or agent is changing an in-scope surface.
- Route each architecture, dependency, portability, or ownership question through `docs/REFERENCES.md`; read the relevant primary sources and at least one comparable implementation when one exists. Also read the applicable contract proofs and dependency or flake decisions. Record the question, exact source revisions, preserved constraints, rejected approaches, decision, and cheapest check in this Bead. Reuse prior evidence only when the question and exact revision still match.

## Scope

In scope:
- `components/eon-alpha-v1.json`, the complete `eon-manifest` crate, and focused graph tests.
- Version reporting and every Nix assertion or package identity derived from the graph.
- EON-C1 through EON-C4 manifest and identity claims, exact child revisions, contracts, interfaces, roles, artifacts, and launch inputs.
- Checks for duplicate truth, missing invariants, unbounded inputs, path neutrality, and replacement cost.

Out of scope:
- Implementing, fixing, refactoring, or editing repository files.
- Adding or changing product contracts, dependencies, compatibility promises, or deferred features.
- Auditing behavior owned by another repository beyond verifying the consumed boundary.
- Creating remediation Beads unless the user separately authorizes a planning-only batch.

## Audit method

1. Record governing instructions, tracker state, accepted contract proofs, and immutable subject identity: clean HEAD, or HEAD plus a SHA-256 of the tracked binary diff and hashes of every in-scope untracked file. Preserve the exact dirty paths.
2. Read every in-scope owner, its direct callers and consumers, meaningful tests, contract rows, reference decisions, and dependency decisions.
3. Trace the observable flow end to end and audit correctness, failures, bounds, security boundaries, performance, tests, ownership, dependencies, portability, DX, and documentation.
4. Run a fresh-eyes correctness pass, then a separate simplification and ownership pass. Reject style preferences, speculative features, accepted tradeoffs, and duplicates of existing Beads.
5. Vet each remaining finding against exact file:line evidence and record impact, effort (S/M/L), implementation risk, confidence, the cheapest falsifying check, and why it merits action.
6. Repeat the complete review after any material planning correction or subject-snapshot change. Converge only when a final full pass over one unchanged recorded snapshot finds no additional actionable finding beyond the recorded set.
7. Record either the vetted findings or an explicit no-finding result in this Bead with the audited revision, commands, failures, and remaining proof limits.

## Acceptance

- The audit covers the complete stated subsystem and adjacent boundaries, not only recent diffs.
- Every finding is concrete, reproducible or directly evidenced, ownership-routed, and checked against existing Beads.
- No tracked project file or preserved untracked user artifact changes during the audit; generated build outputs do not alter the recorded subject snapshot.
- The final record identifies the exact subject snapshot; any in-scope subject change invalidates prior completion and requires a complete new pass.
- The final pass reports convergence under the declared lenses without widening that claim to runtime or platform behavior not exercised.
- Findings remain recommendations until the user chooses separate remediation work.

## Verification

- `cargo fmt --all --check` should exit 0 on the audited revision.
- `cargo check --locked --workspace` should exit 0 on the audited revision.
- `cargo test --locked --workspace` should exit 0 on the audited revision.
- `cargo clippy --locked --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` should exit 0 on the audited revision.
- `git diff --check` should exit 0 on the audited revision.
- `cargo test --locked -p eon-manifest` should exit 0 on the audited revision.
- `cargo run --locked -p eon-manifest -- components/eon-alpha-v1.json` should exit 0 on the audited revision.
- A prior verification result may be cited instead of rerun only when its recorded subject snapshot, environment, command, and exercised surface match exactly; otherwise rerun it.
- `br sync --flush-only` should persist the audit record without changing implementation.
- Final status and diff inspection should show only the pre-existing worktree plus authorized Beads mutations.

## Stop conditions

- Stop if an active implementation owns or materially changes an in-scope surface.
- Stop if evidence requires a new contract, dependency decision, cross-repository owner change, or scope expansion.
- Stop and report rather than compensating for an upstream or downstream contract gap.

title: Audit Eon cross-subsystem integration
description:
## Contract routing

This is a read-only repository audit. It changes no EON product contract, implements no feature or fix, and authorizes no dependency, compatibility surface, or public behavior. Audit one exact accepted revision and preserve all pre-existing worktree state.

## Why

Feature-local fresh-eyes and simplification passes can converge even when all six owners are locally correct but their contracts, documentation, proofs, or lifecycle composition disagree. Repository integration is a distinct failure domain, so it needs one bounded cross-subsystem review.

## Evidence

- `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:82`: the six internal owners and integration rule are explicit
- `docs/CONTRACTS.md:10`: cross-repository contracts and proof status share one index
- `README.md:10`: the user-facing alpha claim spans every subsystem
- `crates/eon/tests/workspace_control.rs:103`: the strongest local process test crosses runtime, workspace, EONW, and Orbit launch boundaries

## Prerequisites and reference gate

- All six declared local subsystem audits must be complete.
- As a cross-repository prerequisite, the completed Orbit and Venus integration-audit records must cover the exact child contract and source revisions selected by Eon's component graph. The trackers are separate, so record those IDs and revisions in this Bead; stop on a missing or mismatched child audit instead of treating a local check as child proof.
- Route unresolved architecture, dependency, portability, or ownership questions through `docs/REFERENCES.md`, the applicable contract proofs, and exact child sources. Record the question, exact source revisions, preserved constraints, rejected approaches, decision, and cheapest check. Reuse prior evidence only when the question and exact revision still match.

## Scope

title: Prove the smallest useful Nix-only Eon Linux composition
description:
Contracts:
EON-C1, EON-C3, and EON-C4. This slice changes no agent-specific product contract.

Goal:
Prove one usable Linux vertical slice through one Nix-managed path. Eon launches an accepted Venus and Orbit pair, exposes Helix, Yazi, and Ratconfig through their owned contracts, preserves one configuration path, reports exact component versions, and exercises one real coding-agent CLI as an ordinary long-running process inside the accepted session boundary.

Agent-first evidence:
Agents are strategically central to the intended product, but this first composition does not invent an agent model, provider integration, dashboard, observer, control protocol, or compatibility promise. It proves only that a real selected coding-agent process can run useful work, survive Venus loss, and remain coherently reachable through Orbit. Record the exact CLI identity and workflow. Do not record credentials, secrets, private prompts, or sensitive terminal output as planning evidence.

Before code:
Review the accepted child contracts and exact proof revisions. State the process tree, configuration ownership, failure behavior, Nix composition boundary, and cheapest integration check. Classify exact current Herdr and VS Code Agent Host evidence as comparison for client-independent agent work, not as dependencies or inherited scope. Run the crate and tool gate for every proposed runtime dependency.

Scope:
Keep the alpha Nix-only and one-session. The agent CLI may be supplied by the dogfood environment and need not enter the component manifest. Agent identity, semantic status, machine-readable actions, observers, attention UI, multiple sessions, sidebars, popups, plugins, remote targets, Home Manager, direct bundles, installers, extra package channels, and new child recovery contracts require separately approved contracts or later slices.
design:
Use the existing one-session composition and accepted Orbit/Venus contracts. The real agent scenario is an acceptance workload, not a reason to add provider-specific code.

Start one selected current coding-agent CLI on a bounded task in a disposable or explicitly chosen repository/worktree. Observe authoritative process and terminal behavior only. Venus disconnects or exits while useful work remains active; Orbit and the PTY stay alive; a restarted Venus coherently reattaches; the user can continue interaction; and the task reaches a visible completion or failure outcome.

Do not infer working, blocked, waiting, completed, or failed semantic agent state from process names, terminal titles, or scraped output. Until an explicit provider-owned signal and Eon normalization contract exist, semantic agent state is unknown. This slice may record human-observed workflow friction without creating an API or state model.

Power Failure Resumer remains required evidence for Eon-owned interruption and recovery UX. acceptance_criteria:
1. The user activates Eon only after exact accepted Orbit and Venus integration revisions exist, and one Nix flake path builds and installs the composed alpha in a clean Nix-enabled user environment.
2. Eon launches the accepted component set, preserves one configuration path, and reports exact component versions from the canonical manifest.
3. A user can launch, use, detach, reattach, and stop the composed terminal session.
4. One real coding-agent CLI at an exact recorded version performs a bounded useful task inside the Orbit session. Venus disconnects or exits while the task remains active; the Orbit process, PTY, and agent process survive; restarted Venus coherently reattaches; and the user can continue interaction to an observed completion or failure.
5. The agent workload changes no provider support promise, component graph, agent API, agent-state contract, observer role, or Orbit/Venus protocol. Credentials and sensitive terminal content are excluded from recorded evidence.
6. Evidence distinguishes authoritative process lifecycle from provider semantic state. Missing provider-authored state is reported as unknown rather than inferred from terminal text, titles, timing, or process names.
7. Normal runtime use invokes no Nix evaluator and persists no Nix store path as component identity.
8. Venus exit and restart preserve the running Orbit session. Eon relaunch, Orbit restart, machine restart, and partial-child failure preserve only state declared durable by accepted child contracts and report every other loss explicitly.
9. Eon contains policy and adapters only; ownership review finds no copied terminal, protocol, rendering, editor, file-manager, Ratconfig, or agent-provider state.
10. Fresh-session dogfood records exact component and agent identities, safe commands, platform, process/lifecycle observations, limitations, and friction without publishing secrets or unsupported performance claims.
11. Canonical Nix or Lix checks, focused integration checks, and repository verification pass.
12. Sidebars, agent dashboards, machine-readable agent actions, observers, multiple sessions, plugins, remote execution, direct distribution, and new recovery behavior remain outside this slice.
13. The same exact Orbit/Venus pair is dogfooded through long primary history, rapid wheel input, byte-producing-key return to live, wrapped Unicode and wide-grapheme selection, explicit copy, resize and reflow, alternate-screen Neovim and Yazi, application mouse mode, DEC 1007, Venus loss, and coherent reattachment. orb-bi4.6 cites this evidence instead of duplicating the composition.
notes: Accepted Nix-only x86_64 Linux alpha. EON-C1 icon identity is proved at 712c0834691c58b07e56494de25f98670b6a882e; EON-C2 through EON-C4 retain their indexed proofs. The exact component graph, runtime ownership, checks, artifact identities, lifecycle dogfood, agent-process evidence, limitations, and candidate corrections are recorded in append-only comments and docs/CONTRACTS.md. No provider contract, workspace, direct distribution, macOS implementation, or restart persistence was added.

Question and smallest observable contract:
Consumer: one Linux alpha user installing the Eon flake. Trigger: run the installed eon command with no subcommand, attach, versions, or config-path. Result: one foreground Eon supervisor starts exactly the accepted Orbit server and transient Venus client, injects one explicit socket plus resolved child artifacts, exposes Helix and Yazi in the Orbit shell, uses one Eon configuration root, and reports stable manifest identities. Important failures: missing resolved inputs, unsafe runtime directory, Orbit startup/socket timeout, Venus spawn/exit, Orbit exit, and incompatible graph must be explicit. Closing Venus leaves Orbit and its PTY/agent process alive while the foreground supervisor remains; eon attach starts only Venus against that socket. Interrupting the foreground supervisor is the explicit alpha stop path. Orbit or machine restart loses undeclared process state and is never described as recovery.

Accepted owners and exact evidence:
- Canonical Eon manifest proof c9e898c9ff889c2be4d4381a20676291bab65b49 and artifact SHA-256 d8d3035b9b62d00267c6ea81dd40d402fd918ef5295071d220c0f1a100689faf remain the only component graph.

Source inspection confirms yazelix-orbit serve [SOCKET] [-- COMMAND...] owns the PTY/shell, removes only its own socket, accepts one presentation client, and handles SIGINT/SIGTERM/SIGHUP. Its libghostty-vt 0.2.1 build pins Ghostty a887df42c56f6de86c0fe6da9c4eeca37931e083 and exposes GHOSTTY_SOURCE_DIR/GHOSTTY_ZIG_SYSTEM_DIR for sandboxed Nix builds.

Required comparison evidence:
- Power Failure Resumer at 732313f467cbdae293dcd7a1de6a923a8274e278, MIT. Independently useful mechanism: discover once, expose confidence/ambiguity, preview a frozen plan, apply idempotently, verify the result, and report partial failure. Consequence here: Eon reports only observed child/process failures and no automatic recovery. Rejected: mtime/process inference, Ghostty/AppleScript drivers, provider resume commands, Python/shell architecture, and machine-restart claims.
- Herdr current master at 50ddc06f00ec69ede35fd5488a260dec2b74e98a, Apache-2.0, with v0.8.0 as latest release. Independently useful mechanism: server-owned real terminal processes survive client detach and reattach. Its exact session-state docs distinguish live detach from snapshot restore, screen replay, native agent resume, and experimental handoff. Consequence: Eon relies only on Orbit live ownership and labels provider semantic state unknown. Rejected: workspaces/tabs/panes, multi-client behavior, terminal ownership, persisted screen/layout, restart reconstruction, live handoff, remote attach, plugins, socket APIs, agent detection, and provider integrations.
- Microsoft vscode-docs at 74f6c45c91823e59b72d0a60787fccf482900023, exact agent-host.md approved 2026-08-05. Independently useful mechanism: a host-owned process/session can continue without a transient client. Consequence: the real agent remains an ordinary Orbit PTY child rather than a Venus child. Rejected: AHP, JSON-RPC/WebSocket, adapters, normalized agent sessions, multi-client control, remote hosts, client tools, worktree UI, and provider support.
- Yazelix Nova at 124308bfa128203f843839346c88296cd266568a. Rejected: Nova identity, runtime, configuration schema, component set, Home Manager, Zellij, and its larger wrapper/tool graph.
No reference source is copied or adapted. Inspection-only use does not import license obligations into Eon; local Nix source builds retain each source license, while redistribution obligations remain astra-db8.7 or later work.

Selected process, state, and configuration ownership:
eon foreground supervisor
├─ yazelix-orbit serve <explicit socket>
│  └─ Orbit-owned PTY shell → optional ordinary coding-agent process
└─ yazelix-venus <same socket>

Nix resolves paths and constructs the installed wrapper. Rust owns launch order, bounded socket readiness, version diagnostics, the one configuration root, and failure messages. Orbit owns PTY/process/terminal/session/socket semantics. Venus owns native client lifecycle and failure UX. The supervisor keeps no terminal or agent state and persists no store path. Nix injects EON_ORBIT and EON_VENUS plus PATH and TERMINFO_DIRS; Rust treats those values as opaque paths. The configuration root is EON_CONFIG_HOME when explicitly supplied, otherwise XDG_CONFIG_HOME/eon or HOME/.config/eon; children receive that root as XDG_CONFIG_HOME. Runtime sockets use EON_RUNTIME_DIR, otherwise XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/eon, otherwise a private temp/effective-UID directory. Linux packaging is an isolated platform dependency; the Rust runtime path and libc effective-UID seam remain Unix-neutral and credible for macOS.

Crate and tool decision:
- New Eon launcher crate: one local eon-manifest dependency. It reuses the already accepted serde 1.0.228 / serde_json 1.0.150 closure through the validator and adds no parser, CLI, async, process-supervisor, logging, signal, or agent dependency.
- libc 0.2.189, exact crates.io pin, MIT OR Apache-2.0: selected only for effective-UID ownership validation in the portable Unix runtime-directory seam. It is already an exact Orbit dependency, adds no unique transitive crate, native library, service, or additional Nix closure, and can be removed when stable std exposes the required identity check or a later platform owner replaces the seam. Environment usernames and Linux-only /proc probing are rejected as weaker or nonportable.
- Nix 2.34.7 flakes with Nixpkgs 567a49d1913ce81ac6e9582e3553dd90a955875f: already selected alpha channel. That pin provides Rust 1.95.0, Zig 0.15.2, and Yazi 26.5.6. buildRustPackage owns Cargo vendoring for Orbit, Venus, and Eon. zig_0_15.fetchDeps owns the exact Ghostty Zig cache. The child Helix flake owns its build. No crane, naersk, rust-overlay at Eon root, container, Home Manager, hosted CI, act, Doodlestein, installer, or release tool is selected.
- Flake inputs duplicate unavoidable resolver coordinates only. Assertions compare every input rev and Nix package source revision with the canonical manifest before a package exists; flake.lock is resolver evidence, never a second product graph. Ratconfig and Ghostty are exact build/reference inputs rather than runtime policy owners.
Estimated new owned surface: roughly 180–300 Rust lines including focused tests and 120–220 Nix lines. Direct runtime dependency delta: one already-present libc crate; no new unique transitive crate. Nix build cost is dominated by the already accepted Orbit Ghostty and Venus graphics closures plus child Helix/Yazi packages. Removal cost is deleting the launcher crate and flake translation while retaining the manifest.

Rejected shapes:
- Nix/shell launcher: would make package glue own durable process and failure policy.
- systemd user service or desktop-entry-first daemonization: Linux-specific lifecycle and hidden background state are unnecessary for the foreground alpha.
- a general supervisor crate, async runtime, clap, daemon library, process table, PID file, recovery database, agent adapter, Ratconfig UI, or provider hook: no accepted behavior needs them.
- invoking nix, parsing store paths, or persisting resolved inputs at runtime: violates EON-C3.
- rebuilding Orbit/Venus behavior, speaking ORBS/ORBF from Eon, or controlling the PTY to stop it: violates EON-C4.
- hosted CI: local Nix/Rust proof is sufficient, so Doodlestein remains comparison-only and no spending surface is created.

First meaningful checks:
1. TDD exact manifest version report and launcher argument/path/failure helpers.
2. A Rust integration process fixture where Venus exits first and Eon demonstrably remains until the Orbit substitute exits; malformed inputs fail before spawn.
3. cargo fmt/check/test/clippy and canonical manifest CLI.
4. nix flake check plus build/install of the exact package; input-revision assertions and installed closure inspection.
5. clean-environment version/config checks and strace/exec observation showing no nix invocation or persisted store-path identity.
6. real packaged Orbit/Venus lifecycle and one exact coding-agent CLI workload, recording only commands/identities, process observations, limitations, and non-sensitive outcomes.

Stop conditions: any required child-contract change, manifest/schema change, new agent/provider state, unsupported source mismatch, macOS-blocking runtime assumption, unapproved dependency owner, or inability to build the accepted exact revisions stops before compensating in Eon.

title: Decide whether Eon agent workspaces need isolated execution targets
description:
## Why

Eon may eventually gain meaningful security and portability value if an agent workspace can run behind an attachable execution target instead of sharing the human host account and filesystem by default. The source discussion combines that useful boundary with agent dashboards, transparent container navigation, microVM lifecycle, and virtualized GPU work; only the execution-target decision is distinct from existing Eon workspace planning.

## Evidence

- Source discussion: https://github.com/luccahuguet/yazelix/discussions/685.
- `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` section `Product boundary` assigns product policy and launch to Eon, persistent sessions, attachment, and transport to Orbit, and native presentation to Venus.
- `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` section `Sequencing` requires Orbit and Venus proof before Eon composition.
- `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` section `Ownership rules` permits Eon boundary adaptation while forbidding duplicate child behavior.
- `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` section `Activation boundary` requires later slices to earn scope through dogfood.
- `eon-pxn` owns local Eon workspace topology and explicitly leaves remote machines outside its first slice.
- Apple Containerization runs Linux containers in separate lightweight VMs on supported macOS hosts: https://github.com/apple/containerization.
- microvm.nix provides NixOS microVMs across multiple Linux hypervisors and vfkit on macOS: https://github.com/microvm-nix/microvm.nix.

## Decision Contract

After the local Eon workspace slice is proven, decide whether one demonstrated agent-security or remote-workflow need justifies an execution-target contract. Compare doing nothing, a restricted host user reached through ordinary SSH, an existing remote SSH host, rootless OCI execution, and one platform-native microVM provider. Start from an explicit threat model and user workflow rather than assuming that containers are always insufficient.

If a target contract is justified, Eon owns target selection and product lifecycle policy, Orbit owns the smallest attachment or transport mechanism, Venus displays target identity and state, and the selected external provider owns VM or container mechanics. A valid decision may be to keep workspaces host-local.

## Scope

In scope:
- Name protected assets, trusted and untrusted actors, credential boundaries, repository access, network policy, persistence, and recovery expectations.
- Evaluate one concrete Linux path and one concrete macOS implication using exact primary-source revisions.
- Define the smallest user-visible target identity, attach, failure, shutdown, and cleanup behavior only if evidence requires it.
- Determine whether existing SSH and provider CLIs satisfy the behavior without an Eon provider framework.
- Route any missing transport mechanism to a separately approved Orbit contract before Eon consumes it.

Out of scope:
- Agent dashboards or panels already covered by workspace and Venus planning.
- VM, container, SSH, filesystem, networking, credential-broker, or sandbox implementation.
- Literal filesystem traversal across hosts, transparent path equivalence, multi-tenant hosting, multiplayer, web/mobile, or automatic repository synchronization.
- Virtio-GPU, GUI applications inside guests, DRM Native Context, GPU sharing, or desktop virtualization.
- Claims that a restricted user, rootless container, or microVM is secure without a stated threat model and platform proof.
- Nova compatibility or changes to the first local Eon workspace contract.

## Implementation Notes

1. Begin only after `eon-pxn` proves useful local multi-session workspace behavior and dogfood records a concrete isolation or remote-target need.
2. Inspect exact revisions of Apple Containerization, microvm.nix, the selected Linux OCI or microVM candidate, and Ptyxis only for terminal-target UX; distinguish OCI image/runtime compatibility from VM lifecycle and terminal attachment.
3. Compare no feature, restricted user plus SSH, remote SSH, rootless OCI, and one microVM shape on ownership, security boundary, startup cost, filesystem and credential exposure, recovery, Linux/macOS fit, dependencies, and removal cost.
4. Prefer direct invocation of an existing provider and an ordinary Orbit endpoint over a generic provider abstraction.
5. Record one recommendation, meaningful rejections, the evidence that would reverse it, and the cheapest isolated proof. Do not implement during this decision bead.

## Verification

- `br show eon-pxn --json` must confirm the local workspace prerequisite and its deferred remote scope.
- `rg -n "Orbit|Venus|Eon|transport|launch" docs/ARCHITECTURE.md docs/CONTRACTS.md` must identify current owners before proposing a contract.
- Every security and platform claim must cite an exact primary-source revision and the exercised platform; compilation or documentation alone is narrower evidence.
- The final Bead state must contain the threat model, ownership map, comparison, recommendation, dependency and tool impact, residual risk, and explicit user decision.
- No runtime, contract index, documentation, dependency, package, CI, or ambient user configuration changes during the decision.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if no dogfooded user need exceeds ordinary host-local or SSH behavior.
- Stop if the proposal requires a generic provider framework before one concrete provider proves value.
- Stop and request a product decision before adding an Orbit transport, security guarantee, credential owner, or supported remote-platform promise.
- Stop if isolation cannot protect the named assets without exposing equal authority through shared credentials, writable mounts, or host control.

## Maintenance Notes

Priority P4 and deferred behind `eon-pxn`. Decision effort M, implementation risk HIGH, confidence HIGH in the ownership boundary and LOW that microVM support will be justified before dogfood. Rejected as separate Beads: hideable agent panel because existing workspace and Venus planning owns it; transparent container-as-directory UX because it misstates the boundary; GPU virtualization because no Eon contract needs it.

title: Decide whether Eon needs an extension system
description:
Contract disposition:
This decision creates no compatibility surface or runtime contract. Eon remains configuration-first and has no general plugin system. If the user later chooses an extension system, approve and index a separate EON contract before implementation.

Current product direction:
Proceed in order: finish and dogfood the core Eon workspace; prove one Eon-owned semantic action registry and make the `eon` CLI its canonical human and agent projection; let one declarative Eon configuration schema and external programs consume those actions; then reconsider plugins only if real recurring needs remain unsolved. Human-readable output and deterministic `--json` output are views of the same action owner, not separate APIs. The action surface and its private local control transport are not a plugin ABI, and configuration must not become an accidental programming language.

Goal:
After eon-pxn proves the workspace, action surface, and declarative-profile boundary, decide whether built-in owner code, the action API, external commands, configuration, or child-owned extension systems are insufficient and a stable Eon extension boundary is justified.

Prerequisites:
- eon-pxn and its activated owner children prove and dogfood the Eon workspace, deterministic action surface, and bounded declarative profile.
- Dogfood records at least two concrete recurring extension cases from different workflows and routes each through the existing owners first.
- The user explicitly activates this decision work; it does not become an implementation frontier automatically.

Ownership:
Eon may own product orchestration, workspace metadata, semantic actions, one product configuration schema and apply policy, and, only if later approved, extension installation, grants, activation, and compatibility. Ratconfig owns reusable configuration editing while consuming the Eon-owned schema and model. Orbit remains plugin-free and owns PTYs, sessions, terminal state, and ORBS/ORBF. Venus owns native rendering and may render only host-defined declarative contributions. Helix and Yazi keep their own extension mechanisms.

Scope:
Research and decide only. Do not add a runtime, SDK, manifest format, extension host, marketplace, plugin API, child-protocol capability, or production code. Do not let external automation or extensions receive raw PTY or protocol frames, fabricate provider state, inject arbitrary UI trees, or bypass separately approved Orbit observation contracts.
design:
Decision ladder:
1. Continue core product work. First-party workspace, tab, pane, attention, graphics, mouse, accessibility, and presentation needs are not plugin evidence.
2. Prove one excellent Eon-owned semantic action registry and its canonical `eon` CLI in eon-pxn. The running supervisor alone owns live workspace and action state behind a private Eon local control endpoint. The CLI exposes stable semantic identities, context-sensitive available actions, typed arguments, structured results, unavailable-action reasons, cancellation, and bounded errors through human-readable output and deterministic `--json` output. It does not address child protocols directly, and begins explicitly versioned and experimental; no stable 1.0 or plugin compatibility promise is implied.
3. Prove one bounded declarative configuration system over the same owner-authored actions. It may describe workspace and launch profiles, keybindings, named action sequences, explicit environment and working-directory inputs, and accepted presentation choices. It has one Eon-owned schema and Ratconfig editing. It does not gain loops, mutable variables, asynchronous callbacks, arbitrary code, custom widget trees, raw terminal control, or a second state owner. External commands using the action surface are the escape hatch.
4. Reopen the plugin decision only when two recurring cases cannot be expressed safely by the first three rungs or a child-owned extension system.

Required comparison:
A. Keep built-ins plus child-owned extension mechanisms.
B. Use the canonical `eon` CLI and the same narrow action protocol from external tools or commands without Eon-owned extension discovery, installation, activation, hosting, SDK promises, or plugin compatibility.
C. Use schema-backed declarative Eon configuration over the action API.
D. Add a plugin system using one of the credible architectures below.

Plugin architecture candidates, only after dogfood earns them:
1. Out-of-process extension executables over the same bounded framed local action protocol. Their implementation language is private and unrestricted; Eon promises the protocol, not supported languages or SDKs. This is the preferred first candidate for trusted local extensions because it reuses the action owner, fits Eon process supervision and Nix-pinned executables, and isolates crashes. Process separation alone is not an authority boundary; ambient user authority and OS sandboxing remain explicit.
2. WebAssembly Components with WIT and a credible runtime only when demonstrated cases require portable untrusted distribution, default-deny capability imports, or resource isolation that the selected process boundary cannot provide. Multiple guest languages are not themselves a product requirement. Record runtime weight, build and startup cost, standards maturity, toolchains, Linux and macOS support, and removal cost.
3. An embedded language runtime only when the demonstrated cases require synchronous or high-frequency in-process callbacks that the external action protocol cannot satisfy. At that point compare no runtime with exact credible languages and require the selected runtime to remove a complete Eon responsibility. Do not choose a language for syntax taste, agent novelty, or programmable configuration alone.

Language and runtime disposition:
Zero, Roto, Steel, Lua, Luau, and other languages remain discovery inputs rather than standing candidates. Zero is useful comparison evidence for semantic graph inspection, checked edits, typed facts, explicit effects, and agent-facing diagnostics, but its current experimental compiled toolchain is not an Eon extension host, stable compatibility boundary, or security sandbox. Reconsider a named language only when a demonstrated extension case and exact current evidence make its runtime uniquely credible.

Native Rust dynamic-library plugins are not a default candidate because they couple compiler and ABI choices to the host and place extension failure in the Eon process. Reconsider them only if exact evidence makes that coupling advantageous.

Reference gate:
Begin with the demonstrated cases, the exact accepted eon-pxn action, CLI, and configuration contracts, and the exact owner mechanisms they consume. First test whether built-ins, child-owned extensions, `eon` CLI composition, bounded wait or events, configuration, or an ordinary external process solve each case. Inspect an out-of-process extension-host precedent only if Eon-owned installation and activation remain necessary. Inspect WebAssembly Components, WIT, and a selected runtime only for a demonstrated untrusted portable-code requirement. Inspect a named embedded language only for a demonstrated synchronous in-process requirement. Compare no new dependency, existing process and protocol facilities, release health, licenses, Linux and macOS support, dependency and compile weight, security posture, owned LOC, compatibility burden, and removal cost. Agent-authoring ergonomics are secondary to ownership, failure isolation, security, portability, and compatibility.

Security and lifecycle gate:
Default-deny filesystem, environment, process spawning, network, clipboard, secrets, raw terminal or protocol data, GPU, windows, webviews, and background execution. Separate read-only observation from mutation. Define memory, wall-time, queue, message, result, log, storage, concurrency, activation, cancellation, crash, restart, and shutdown bounds. An extension-host crash must not terminate Orbit or Venus, and safe mode must disable third-party extensions.

Distribution and compatibility gate:
Start with local or Nix-pinned immutable bundles only. Identity is publisher, name, version, API version, and content hash, never a Nix store path. Permissions match imported capabilities and re-prompt when expanded. Defer a marketplace, arbitrary panels, custom widget trees, remote installation, signing infrastructure, and a multi-language support promise. Define the selected API version policy and make no stable compatibility promise before an explicitly approved 1.0 API.

Stop conditions:
Stop with no plugin feature if built-ins, the action API, external commands, declarative configuration, or child-owned plugins cover the demonstrated needs. Stop if the design needs Orbit plugins, raw ORBS/ORBF access, duplicated terminal or provider state, speculative capability negotiation, ambient authority presented as sandboxing, or a marketplace before local extensions prove value. Stop for explicit user choice before creating a contract or implementation bead.
acceptance_criteria:
1. eon-pxn and its activated owner children prove the core workspace, deterministic action surface, and bounded declarative-profile boundary before this decision starts.
2. Dogfood supplies at least two independent recurring extension cases and explains why built-in owner code, the action API, external commands, declarative configuration, and child-owned plugins do not solve them. First-party tabs, panes, overlays, status items, graphics, mouse behavior, accessibility, and presentation do not count as extension demand.
3. The record distinguishes the Eon-owned action registry and canonical CLI from a plugin system: actions expose semantic state and behavior through human-readable and deterministic structured projections, while extension discovery, installation, activation, hosting, grants, SDK promises, and compatibility remain absent unless explicitly approved. The running supervisor is the sole live action-state owner, and the CLI or external clients never bypass it by speaking child protocols directly.
4. The configuration candidate has one Eon-owned schema and apply policy, is edited through Ratconfig, consumes accepted semantic actions, and contains no arbitrary executable language, loops, mutable callbacks, custom widget trees, raw terminal control, or duplicate state.
5. The comparison grades continuing with built-ins, API plus external tools, declarative configuration, and a plugin system against product value, human and agent usability, architecture, security, portability, dependency cost, compatibility burden, and removal cost.
6. If plugins remain justified, the reference and crate or tool gates start with out-of-process executable extensions over the accepted Eon action protocol. They evaluate WebAssembly Components only for demonstrated portable untrusted-code or isolation needs, and a named embedded runtime only for demonstrated synchronous or high-frequency in-process needs that the external protocol cannot meet. They compare no new dependency and record why Zero or any other language is or is not credible at its exact current revision. Eon makes no supported-language, SDK, or multi-language promise merely because executable or Wasm boundaries permit several implementations.
7. The decision names one owner for identity, installation, activation, grants, actions, UI contributions, state, failures, and compatibility while preserving Orbit, Venus, Ratconfig, Helix, and Yazi ownership.
8. A threat model and capability table cover filesystem, environment, process, network, clipboard, secrets, terminal observation, UI, storage, and background work with deny-by-default behavior. Process separation is not claimed as authority isolation without an OS sandbox.
9. Resource, lifecycle, crash-isolation, safe-mode, Linux and macOS, distribution, upgrade, removal, and API-version policies are explicit and falsifiable.
10. Any proposed plugin proof contains exactly the two demonstrated first-party extensions and checks useful behavior, permission denial, runaway execution, extension crash, incompatible API version, and clean removal.
11. The record estimates owned LOC, dependency weight, compile and runtime cost, maintenance, and permanent compatibility cost and names evidence that would reverse the recommendation.
12. The user explicitly chooses keep built-ins and the CLI/action API only, add declarative configuration only, use a narrow out-of-process extension contract, adopt WebAssembly Components for a demonstrated portable untrusted-code or isolation requirement, adopt a named embedded runtime for a demonstrated in-process requirement, reject plugins, or defer.
13. Closure creates no runtime code, dependency, manifest, protocol change, marketplace, SDK, or compatibility promise.
notes:
User-approved planning direction on 2026-08-08: sequence core product work, a narrow high-quality action API, schema-backed declarative configuration, and only then a plugin decision if dogfood still demonstrates unmet needs.

Current judgment:
- Continue core workspace work: A for the present frontier.
- One Eon-owned semantic action registry with the canonical `eon` CLI for humans and agents: A+, the preferred control and extensibility backbone.
- Bounded declarative configuration and ordinary external programs consuming the same actions: A, the preferred customization and automation layers.
- General plugin system: D at the current product stage, with an A- ceiling only after concrete demand and successful ownership, security, lifecycle, portability, and compatibility gates.

If plugins are later earned, out-of-process executables over the accepted action protocol are the preferred first candidate for trusted local extensions. Their language remains a private implementation detail rather than an Eon support promise. WebAssembly Components are conditional on demonstrated untrusted portable-code or isolation requirements. An embedded runtime is conditional on demonstrated synchronous in-process requirements that external actions cannot meet. No architecture, SDK, supported guest language, or durable second language is selected by this planning decision.

Priority P4 remains intentional. This work follows the eon-pxn workspace and action proof rather than competing with Orbit, Venus, or the first Eon workspace frontier.

Feature-horizon boundary: eon-pxn owns bounded native horizontal tabs, visual vertical accordion panes, semantic actions, and declarative workspace or profile pressure as first-party product architecture. Generic overlays, floating terminal popups, arbitrary split trees, fixed status items, semantic mouse routing, accessibility focus, and graphics remain first-party owner concerns rather than plugin evidence.

Planning effort M; implementation risk HIGH because every published capability becomes a security and compatibility surface. Confidence HIGH in API-first and configuration-first sequencing, HIGH in deferring plugins, and LOW that an embedded runtime is justified before concrete cases exist.

First-principles language disposition approved on 2026-08-08:
- Eon needs one semantic action owner and canonical CLI, not an Eon-specific plugin language.
- Zero is retained as high-value comparison evidence for agent-queryable semantic interfaces, not selected as a dependency or extension runtime.
- Syntax elegance, static typing, and single-language ecosystem preferences do not outrank child ownership, crash isolation, security, portability, protocol stability, and removal cost.
- A language or runtime becomes credible only when dogfood supplies a case that the CLI, external actions, configuration, and child-owned mechanisms cannot solve.

title: License Eon and keep the local runtime current
description:
## Contract routing

This repository-governance, distribution-metadata, and local-delivery task changes no EON product contract. The user selected Apache-2.0 for the whole Eon repository and directed agents to update the user runtime whenever Eon changes.

## Scope

- Add the exact Apache License 2.0 text used by Yazelix Nova; align all Cargo and Nix package metadata and Nix license retention.
- Add one repository-local agent rule: after an accepted Eon change, refresh the active Nix-profile runtime from the current working tree and verify it.
- Render the generated protocol files from pinned clean Starcompass and update the README LOC scorecard.
- Refresh the active eon profile element now.
- Preserve all unrelated dirty work. Do not activate direct distribution, change dependencies, repin components, or interrupt live Sessions.

## Safety boundary

Updating the installed Nix profile is authorized. Stopping or restarting a live Eon supervisor is not automatic because it terminates active Sessions; report the remaining restart requirement unless the user explicitly authorizes interruption.

## Acceptance

- Root LICENSE is byte-for-byte identical to Nova LICENSE at 57b0c8621894c59d058d7ba7d91464864b7c4917.
- Every Eon Cargo package and the built Nix package report Apache-2.0; the artifact retains the license.
- The editable local policy and rendered AGENTS.md require current-working-tree Nix-profile refresh plus exact verification after Eon changes, with the live-session safety boundary.
- Source-backed Starcompass checks and an isolated representative agent trial pass.
- The active eon Nix-profile element resolves to the verified current-working-tree artifact; installed help exposes the current workspace commands and the installed license matches.
- LOC and git diff checks pass; existing running processes remain untouched and are reported stale until restarted.
notes: Complete: Eon is Apache-2.0 throughout; the generated policy requires Nix-profile runtime refresh after accepted changes and forbids invoking another agent for instruction validation unless the user explicitly asks. title: Decide whether a native semantic editor should replace Helix in Eon
description:
Contract disposition:
This decision changes no product contract. EON-C4 currently preserves Helix as the sole owner of editing and language integration. A replace decision requires explicit user approval, an updated ownership architecture, and new or revised indexed EON contracts before implementation. Until then, Helix remains the default editor and Eon owns no editor state.

Goal:
After the first usable Eon composition has been dogfooded, decide whether unique product value justifies replacing Helix with a greenfield Eon-native semantic editor engine. Evaluate the capability replacement alone buys: authoritative addressable buffers, revisions, selections, diagnostics, native editor presentation, and explicit human-agent edit/conflict semantics. Native appearance, component count, or ownership preference alone are insufficient reasons.

Prerequisites:
- eon-ax4 has proved the initial Helix-based Eon composition.
- Dogfood records concrete limitations caused by the editor being behind the PTY and terminal-presentation boundary.
- The user explicitly activates this decision work; it does not become the active implementation frontier automatically.

Reference gate:
Inspect official Helix source at an exact revision, including helix-core, helix-view, helix-term, commands, rendering, language integration, IPC, plugin, and embedding boundaries. Inspect at least one mature native Rust editor and one relevant editor-core or semantic-document precedent at exact revisions. Compare three credible shapes: keep Helix as an opaque Orbit-hosted child; consume a supported upstream semantic or native-frontend boundary if one exists; or build a separate greenfield editor engine consumed by Venus. Record direct source evidence, license implications, portability, dependency and transitive weight, estimated owned LOC, maintenance burden, replacement cost, and material negative results.

Ownership constraints:
- Orbit remains the terminal-session and terminal-state owner; it must not acquire buffers, selections, undo, syntax, diagnostics, or editor lifecycle.
- A new editor engine, if approved, owns document state, revisions, selections, undo, syntax, language integration, safe save, and external-change conflict semantics.
- Venus owns native editor presentation, input, IME, and accessibility without reconstructing editor authority.
- Eon owns workspace policy and composition, not editing mechanics.
- A separate repository does not imply a separate process. Process separation requires a chosen lifecycle contract such as dirty-buffer survival or attachability.

Acceptance:
- Record the exact terminal-bound limitations observed in dogfood and distinguish those requiring replacement from those solvable by configuration or a narrow supported integration.
- State one irreducible user-visible contract that makes replacement worthwhile, or conclude that no such contract exists.
- Produce before-and-after ownership and data-flow maps with no duplicate editor or terminal authority.
- Record the keep, integrate, and greenfield comparison with exact references, dependency implications, rough owned-LOC range, maintenance cost, portability risks, and exit conditions.
- Define the smallest falsifiable proof for the recommended shape; do not implement it without separate user activation.
- Obtain and record an explicit user keep, defer, integrate, or replace decision.

Scope boundary:
This bead authorizes research and a product decision only. It does not create a repository, add runtime code or dependencies, change EON-C4, alter the component manifest, promise Helix compatibility, fork or copy Helix, add persistence or collaboration, or remove Helix. Helix remains the accepted editor until a later explicitly activated implementation bead proves and promotes a replacement.

- Preserve user data and avoid unrequested shell-profile edits.
- Verify on a clean user environment and record artifact size and closure contents.
- Direct and Nix installations report the same component graph and runtime semantics.
- Prepare yazelix.com installation copy without making the website the binary authority.

AppImage, Flatpak, deb, rpm, containers, system repositories, and macOS stay outside this bead.

title: Define the canonical Eon component manifest
description:
Contracts:
EON-C2 and EON-C3.

Goal:
Define one small, human-reviewable manifest that pins exact child revisions, compatibility contracts, and declared package or artifact inputs. Nix consumes this graph during alpha. Later distribution tooling must extend the same graph instead of replacing it.

Reference and tool gate:
Inspect current child release and package metadata plus at least one comparable multi-component manifest. Compare a small hand-owned schema with using existing Nix metadata directly. Record versioning, validation, local LOC, maintenance, and the point at which external release tooling becomes useful. Defer cargo-dist, portable-bundle, and installer evaluation to the direct-distribution gate.

Acceptance:
- The alpha schema names project, revision, contract version, target, package or artifact input, and launch inputs.
- A focused validator rejects incompatible or incomplete component sets.
- One fixture pins the exact owner revisions and contracts required by the alpha: ORB-C1 through ORB-C9, VEN-C1 through VEN-C4, and VEN-C7, their canonical ORBS v2 and ORBF v1 package boundary, plus Helix, Yazi, and Ratconfig. Additional proved contracts may be recorded without becoming activation prerequisites. If preactivation hardening advances an owner proof, pin the final accepted proof rather than preserving an obsolete candidate.
- Eon receives resolved component paths without constructing store paths or invoking a Nix evaluator during normal use.
- Product state records stable component identities instead of resolved store paths.
- docs/CONTRACTS.md records exact proof evidence.

Scope:
Do not require portable artifacts during Nix-only alpha. Do not create a second dependency graph for a package manager or rebuild child behavior in Eon.

Reference and tool gate — EON-C2/EON-C3, before manifest/test/code edits

Question and contract: Eon’s Nix alpha and every later distribution channel need one reviewable graph. Consumer: the astra-db8.3 Nix composition and later approved release tooling. Trigger: loading the manifest for a selected target. Result: exact stable component identities, source revisions, declared outputs, semantic launch inputs, accepted child contracts, and the ORBF v1 / ORBS v2 compatibility edge. Important failures: malformed or duplicate data, unsupported schema, missing or dangling components, incompatible Orbit/Venus revisions or protocol versions, non-immutable Git revisions, absolute artifact paths, and any persisted /nix/store path. The manifest owns the graph; the validator enforces it but does not resolve, build, launch, or reinterpret child behavior.

Required child evidence:
- Eon Sessions accepted handoff 00b136318bea13e3f08d490468f069de6f6b9bd2: Cargo package yazelix-orbit 0.1.0, private orbit-protocol 0.1.0, ORB-C1–C9 proof 9d6d2bb37f20ab4ad9e186c7bc715eabef43e757, ORB-C10 proof 292b2451c9a1d99390334771a681c7f481c996f2, Rust 1.96.0, Zig 0.15.2, pinned Ghostty a887df42c56f6de86c0fe6da9c4eeca37931e083, and repository-owned terminfo/eon.terminfo. These licenses permit the planned source-build/package use under their own conditions. This change copies no source from any component and creates no distribution artifact, so attribution/bundle obligations remain for astra-db8.3 and later distribution work.

Required comparable manifest evidence: Yazelix Nova flake.nix and schema-7 flake.lock at exact commit 124308bfa128203f843839346c88296cd266568a. The flake declares a multi-component Nix graph, the generated lock pins Git revisions and NAR hashes, and package assertions bind selected versions. Useful mechanisms: exact revisions, source hashes where the resolver has them, explicit target outputs, and one graph consumed by checks. Rejected surrounding scope: Nova’s component set, runtime, Home Manager variants, store-path substitutions, and generated lock as Eon product identity. Nix 2.34.7’s flake model creates flake.lock from Nix inputs; making it canonical would make the alpha channel own product identity and force later direct tooling to reconstruct Eon policy. Format and tool comparison:
- Hand-owned JSON plus a standard-library validator: selected. comments.text:
Reference-gate correction, crate gate, and rebaseline — 2026-08-07 America/Sao_Paulo

User direction after the original gate: the Yazelix stack is Rust-only in general; consider exceptions from first principles, document the reasoning, and continue. Accepted policy for this Bead: durable Eon product behavior and repository tooling are Rust; Nix owns packaging; shell is reserved for irreducible process glue; Python remains suitable only for disposable exploration whose code is not retained. The earlier failing Python-first test is discarded evidence and will be removed before Rust implementation. This is a material code-shape change, so this comment rebaselines the run before Cargo, manifest, test, or generated-lock edits.

Correction to comment 7: its claim that TOML would require another Nix parse path was wrong. Nix provides builtins.fromTOML. JSON is still selected because this artifact is a strict machine-owned dependency graph that needs no comments or TOML-specific types, Nix and Rust both consume it directly, and JSON keeps the persisted surface narrower. The obsolete statement remains in append-only history and is not relied on.

First-principles decision:
- The validator is durable policy: it defines which component graphs Eon accepts. Language consistency therefore affects ownership, review, build reproducibility, onboarding, and removal cost, not just initial LOC.
- Rust gives compile-time schema ownership, one project toolchain, one test/format/lint path, and a reusable library boundary for the later Nix composition without making Nix or shell reinterpret the graph.
- Python would save initial code but introduce a second durable toolchain and split conventions for one small repository. That lifecycle cost exceeds its local brevity here.
- Go would add a second compiled ecosystem with no concurrency, deployment, or service advantage. TypeScript would add Node/package-manager state without a web runtime. Shell/jq would make cross-reference validation less legible. A handwritten JSON parser would avoid crates only by rebuilding a difficult trust boundary.
- Nova at exact commit 124308bfa128203f843839346c88296cd266568a is the local precedent: 47 tracked Rust files, no tracked Python/Go/TypeScript/JavaScript, standard-library Rust utilities compiled directly in flake.nix, and Rust serde_json/toml contract checks. Eon follows the durable-tooling principle, not Nova implementation details.

Crate gate:
- serde 1.0.228 with derive, exact crates.io pin, MIT OR Apache-2.0: owns typed deserialization and unknown-field rejection.

title: Prove Home Manager and direct-release parity with Nix Eon
description:
Contract:
EON-C6.

Goal:
Keep the proven Nix package as a supported channel after direct distribution and let Home Manager consume that same package and product contract.

Prerequisites:
- eon-ohh proves the first direct Linux bundle against the same canonical component manifest and accepted runtime semantics.
- The user separately activates Home Manager integration; direct-distribution graduation does not activate another channel automatically.

Reference and tool gate:
Inspect the exact supported Home Manager revision and its official package, module, option, activation, state-version, upgrade, and removal contracts. Compare no Eon-specific integration with `home.packages` consumption and the smallest thin Eon module justified by demonstrated configuration needs. Record Linux target support, evaluation and activation failures, ownership of user files, dependency weight, local LOC, compatibility policy, and removal cost. Reject any shape that creates a Home-Manager-only component graph, settings owner, runtime behavior, or release identity.

Acceptance:
- The original Nix package, Home Manager integration, and direct release consume the same exact component revisions and compatibility metadata.
- Version diagnostics match across channels.
- Runtime behavior and configuration ownership remain channel-independent.
- A clean Nix profile and Home Manager evaluation pass without requiring the direct installer.
- Direct-install users need no Nix evaluator or store.

Scope:
Do not maintain a Home-Manager-only component graph, runtime contract, or feature. This bead does not expand the Nix-only alpha surface.

title: Graduate Eon from Nix-only dogfood to direct distribution
description:
Decision gate:
Keep Eon Nix-only through alpha and early dogfood. Do not begin portable archive, installer, signing, Homebrew, or package-matrix implementation until the user explicitly activates direct distribution through this Bead.

Contract:
EON-C5, informed by EON-C1 through EON-C4 and every accepted active-work lifecycle contract.

Required evidence:
- The Nix composition launches one accepted Orbit and Venus pair with Helix, Yazi and Ratconfig through their owned contracts.
- Sustained fresh-session dogfood covers launch, detach, reattach, configuration, diagnostics, upgrades, Venus restart, declared Eon relaunch semantics, partial-child failure, and the real coding-agent lifecycle required by eon-ax4.
- An upgrade cannot silently terminate an active Orbit-backed agent or other long-running process.
- Orbit or machine restart persistence remains an explicit limitation unless a separate accepted child contract proves it.
- Exact component revisions have no open P0 or P1 integration defect.
- Product code accepts explicit component paths, invokes no Nix evaluator during normal use, and persists stable component identity instead of store paths.
- The component manifest describes the accepted product without using derivation identity as a runtime contract.
- The team has capacity to maintain artifacts, verification, safe staging, upgrades, rollback and removal.

Decision record:
Compare staying Nix-only longer with one direct Linux bundle. Name the user value, first target, release owner, expected CI and maintenance cost, active-work upgrade policy, tool-gate evidence, and deferred features.

Scope:
This Bead authorizes one direct-distribution decision. It does not implement a bundle, live handoff, restart persistence, provider integration, or another package channel. If safe replacement requires a new Orbit lifecycle contract, route that separately before distribution proceeds.
design:
Treat active agent and terminal work as user data at risk during upgrades.

Before approving direct distribution, exercise the exact update path while an ordinary long-running process and the selected real coding-agent workload are active. Replacing Venus may reconnect through accepted contracts. Replacing Orbit must not be assumed safe: when no accepted live-handoff contract exists, stage or defer the incompatible Orbit update until affected sessions stop, or require explicit informed confirmation naming the processes and state that will be lost. Automatic or background update must never kill active work silently.

Inspect exact current Herdr session-state and live-handoff behavior as comparison evidence for preserving PTYs across runtime replacement, plus official platform update and process-lifecycle sources relevant to the selected bundle. This selects no handoff architecture. A live-handoff, external PTY owner, daemon-restart persistence, or agent-native restore path requires its own Orbit or Eon contract and proof.

The release tool gate still compares staying Nix-only, local owned or Nix-native commands, one direct Linux bundle and credible maintained tooling. Record artifacts, verification, signing or attestation, rollback, removal, CI cost and the user hard spending boundary.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The Nix-only Eon composition has sustained fresh-session dogfood for launch, detach, reattach, configuration, diagnostics, upgrades, Venus restart, declared Eon relaunch semantics, partial-child failure, and one real coding-agent lifecycle.
2. The exact upgrade path is exercised while both an ordinary long-running process and a real agent process are active.
3. No upgrade, rollback or automatic update silently terminates an active Orbit-backed process. If Orbit replacement cannot preserve it, the update is staged or deferred until sessions stop, or explicit confirmation names the affected sessions, processes, unpersisted state and exact loss.
4. Orbit and machine restart persistence is either backed by a separately accepted child contract or recorded as an explicit limitation. Distribution code does not simulate or imply it.
5. Any proposed live handoff, external PTY owner, agent-native restoration or new recovery behavior is routed to a separate approved owner contract before distribution consumes it.
6. The accepted component set has no open P0 or P1 integration defect.
7. The accepted Venus revision proves structured terminal accessibility through ven-q3w with bounded scene-derived semantics, keyboard and assistive-technology actions, failure UX and fresh Linux screen-reader dogfood.
8. Product code invokes no Nix evaluator during normal use and persists no store path as stable component identity.
9. The component manifest describes the accepted product without derivation identity as a runtime contract.
10. The tool gate compares staying Nix-only with one direct Linux bundle and records maintenance, CI, active-work staging, artifact verification, rollback and removal costs.
11. The user explicitly approves distribution graduation and selects the first direct target.
12. The decision records the exact component manifest, Orbit and Venus proof revisions, agent-work and accessibility dogfood environments, proof commands, active-work upgrade policy, known limitations, artifact authority and rollback condition.
13. Approval covers one direct-distribution slice and no additional package channel or runtime feature.
notes:
Eon alpha and early dogfood remain Nix-only. Direct distribution is a later adoption path behind this explicit gate, and runtime ownership stays distribution-neutral.

Active agent runs raise the cost of a careless update from inconvenience to lost work. Safe staging or explicit loss confirmation is therefore part of distribution acceptance even while Orbit restart persistence and live handoff remain unimplemented.

Exact current Herdr live-handoff behavior is comparison evidence, not a selected dependency or required architecture. Doodlestein Self Releaser remains required release-tool comparison evidence under the existing hosted Actions spending constraints.
